title: Αἰγίς
about: Thoas of Aetolia marvels that Hector has risen again, and urges the army to send the common mass back to the ships while the best men stand against him. They obey and array the battle, but Hector comes on at the head of the Trojans, with Apollo before him in a cloud, shaking the aegis. While it is held still the missiles fall on both sides; when the god shakes it and shouts, the Achaeans lose their courage and scatter like cattle before wild beasts. Hector and Aeneas and others kill a series of Achaean leaders, and Hector forbids the Trojans to stop for spoils. Apollo then tramples the banks of the ditch into a causeway and begins to pull down the wall as a child jumbles together the playthings he has built in the sand, while Nestor prays to Zeus to save the Achaeans.

sentences.t:
τοῖσι δ’ ἔπειτ’ ἀγόρευε Θόας Ἀνδραίμονος υἱός,
Αἰτωλῶν ὄχ’ ἄριστος ἐπιστάμενος μὲν ἄκοντι
ἐσθλὸς δ’ ἐν σταδίῃ· ἀγορῇ δέ ἑ παῦροι Ἀχαιῶν
νίκων, ὁππότε κοῦροι ἐρίσσειαν περὶ μύθων·
sentences.l:
To them then was declaring Thoas, Andraemon’s son,
of the Aetolians by far the best, skilled with the javelin
and good in the standing fight; and in assembly few of the Achaeans
beat him, whenever young men rivalled one another over words;
sentences.i: Then Thoas, son of Andraemon, declared to them. He was far the best of the Aetolians, skilled with the javelin and good in the fight where men stand their ground, and in the assembly few of the Achaeans beat him whenever young men rivalled one another over words.
sentences.n: ἀγόρευε ‘was declaring’ is the imperfect of ἀγορεύω, to speak in a public gathering, and Θόας Ἀνδραίμονος υἱός ‘Thoas, Andraemon’s son’ is its subject; the rest of the unit tells who he is. ἐπιστάμενος ‘skilled’ takes the dative ἄκοντι ‘with the javelin’, and ἐν σταδίῃ ‘in the standing fight’ has ὑσμίνῃ understood: close fighting in which men hold their ground. ὄχ’ is ὄχα ‘by far’. In line 283 ἑ is ‘him’, and in line 284 νίκων is the imperfect of νικάω without its augment; the optative ἐρίσσειαν after ὁππότε makes the clause a repeated event, ‘whenever …’.

sentences.t: ὅ σφιν ἐϋφρονέων ἀγορήσατο καὶ μετέειπεν·
sentences.l: he, well-disposed in mind toward them, addressed-the-assembly and spoke among them:
sentences.i: with kindly intent toward them he addressed the assembly and spoke among them:
sentences.n: ὅ is ‘he’: in Homer this is a pronoun, not ‘which’. σφιν is ‘to them’, and ἐϋφρονέων the participle of ἐϋφρονέω ‘be well-disposed’. ἀγορήσατο ‘addressed the assembly’ and μετέειπεν ‘spoke among them’ together introduce the speech, a line the poet uses elsewhere. Thoas’s words begin in the next unit.

sentences.t:
ὢ πόποι ἦ μέγα θαῦμα τόδ’ ὀφθαλμοῖσιν ὁρῶμαι,
οἷον δ’ αὖτ’ ἐξαῦτις ἀνέστη κῆρας ἀλύξας
Ἕκτωρ·
sentences.i: “Ah, this is truly a great wonder that I behold with my own eyes: how Hector has risen again, once more, having escaped the fates of death.
sentences.n: ὢ πόποι is an exclamation of dismay or wonder, and ἦ is ‘truly’. τόδ’ ‘this’ is the object of ὁρῶμαι ‘I behold’, the epic form with a middle ending, and ὀφθαλμοῖσιν is the epic dative plural ‘with my eyes’. In the next line οἷον is the neuter accusative used as an exclamation, ‘how’, and the wonder is that Hector got up again. ἀνέστη is the aorist ‘stood up’, κῆρας is the plural of κήρ ‘death-fate’ (not κῆρ ‘heart’), and ἀλύξας is the aorist participle of ἀλύσκω ‘escape’. Ἕκτωρ is held back to the end of the sentence.

sentences.t:
ἦ θήν μιν μάλα ἔλπετο θυμὸς ἑκάστου
χερσὶν ὑπ’ Αἴαντος θανέειν Τελαμωνιάδαο.
sentences.l:
Truly, indeed, the heart of each man greatly expected
him to die under the hands of Ajax, Telamon’s son.
sentences.i: Surely the heart of every man expected him to die at the hands of Ajax, son of Telamon.
sentences.n: ἦ θήν is an emphatic pair, ‘truly, indeed’, and μιν ‘him’, Hector, is the subject of the infinitive θανέειν. ἔλπετο is the imperfect of ἔλπομαι ‘expect’, and θυμὸς ἑκάστου ‘the heart of each man’ is its subject. θανέειν is the epic aorist infinitive of θνῄσκω (Attic θανεῖν), ‘to die’. ὑπό with χερσίν ‘under the hands of’ means ‘by’. Τελαμωνιάδαο is the epic genitive of the patronymic ‘son of Telamon’, here added to Αἴαντος to say which Ajax.

sentences.t:
ἀλλά τις αὖτε θεῶν ἐρρύσατο καὶ ἐσάωσεν
Ἕκτορ’, ὃ δὴ πολλῶν Δαναῶν ὑπὸ γούνατ’ ἔλυσεν,
ὡς καὶ νῦν ἔσσεσθαι ὀΐομαι·
sentences.i: Some one of the gods has rescued Hector and saved him again, the man who has loosed the knees of many Danaans; and I suspect it will be so now as well.
sentences.n: ἀλλά ‘but’ sets the real cause against what each man expected: a god rescued him. ἐρρύσατο is the aorist middle of ῥύομαι ‘rescue’ (the doubled ρ comes from a lost consonant), and ἐσάωσεν the aorist of σαόω ‘save’. γούνατ’ ἔλυσεν ‘loosed the knees’ is the poet’s way of saying ‘killed’: the knees give way. In line 292 ὡς is ‘so’, and ἔσσεσθαι is the infinitive ‘to be’ after ὀΐομαι ‘I suspect’; the sense is that Hector will do the same again now.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ ἄτερ γε
Ζηνὸς ἐριγδούπου πρόμος ἵσταται ὧδε μενοινῶν.
sentences.l:
for not without Zeus, loud-crashing,
the champion stands thus, being minded.
sentences.i: For this champion would not take his stand like this, so intent, without loud-crashing Zeus.
sentences.n: γάρ gives the reason for the suspicion: such a champion would not stand there without Zeus. ἄτερ ‘without’ takes the genitive Ζηνός, from the stem Ζην- of the name Zeus. ἐριγδούπου ‘loud-crashing’ is the epithet the Odyssey also gives him, and πρόμος ‘champion’ is Hector. ὧδε is ‘thus’ and μενοινῶν the participle of μενοινάω ‘be minded’; the verb is used here with nothing said of what he is set on.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἄγεθ’ ὡς ἂν ἐγὼν εἴπω πειθώμεθα πάντες.
sentences.l: But come, as I may say let us obey, all of us.
sentences.i: But come, let us all do as I say.
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγεθ’ ‘but come’ is the opening of a proposal. ὡς ἂν ἐγὼν εἴπω is ‘as I may say’, with ἄν and the subjunctive giving ‘however I tell you’. πειθώμεθα is the subjunctive of πείθομαι, ‘let us obey’, and πάντες ‘all of us’. The line is used elsewhere in the poem.

sentences.t: πληθὺν μὲν ποτὶ νῆας ἀνώξομεν ἀπονέεσθαι·
sentences.l: The multitude to the ships let us order to go back;
sentences.i: Let us order the mass of the army to go back to the ships;
sentences.n: πληθύν is the crowd of ordinary fighters, set against the best men of the next line by μέν … δέ. ἀνώξομεν is a first-person plural of ἀνώγω ‘order’ and, like the other first-person plurals in this speech, means ‘let us’. ποτί is πρός ‘to’, and ἀπονέεσθαι is the infinitive of ἀπονέομαι ‘go back’.

sentences.t:
αὐτοὶ δ’, ὅσσοι ἄριστοι ἐνὶ στρατῷ εὐχόμεθ’ εἶναι,
στήομεν, εἴ κεν πρῶτον ἐρύξομεν ἀντιάσαντες
δούρατ’ ἀνασχόμενοι·
sentences.i: and let us ourselves, all who claim to be the best in the army, make our stand, to see if we can hold him back first, meeting him with our spears held up;
sentences.n: αὐτοὶ δ’ ‘but we ourselves’ answers the μέν of the last unit. ὅσσοι … εὐχόμεθ’ εἶναι is ‘as many as claim to be’: εὔχομαι can mean ‘pray’, ‘boast’ or ‘claim’, and here it is ‘claim’. στήομεν is the aorist subjunctive of ἵστημι, ‘let us take our stand’, and εἴ κεν with ἐρύξομεν ‘if we may hold him back’ gives a hope, ‘to see whether’; the object ‘him’ (Hector) is left out. ἀντιάσαντες is ‘meeting him’ and ἀνασχόμενοι ‘holding up’, both aorist participles.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ οἴω καὶ μεμαῶτα
θυμῷ δείσεσθαι Δαναῶν καταδῦναι ὅμιλον.
sentences.l:
and him, I suspect, even though eager,
in heart will fear to go down into the throng of the Danaans.”
sentences.i: As for him, I suspect that eager as he is he will be afraid in his heart to plunge into the throng of the Danaans.”
sentences.n: τόν ‘him’ is Hector, put first for contrast. οἴω is ὀΐω ‘I suspect’, the same verb as ὀΐομαι earlier in the speech. μεμαῶτα is the perfect participle of μέμονα ‘be eager’, and καί before it gives ‘even though eager’. δείσεσθαι is the future infinitive of δείδω ‘fear’, and καταδῦναι the aorist infinitive of καταδύω ‘go down into’, with ὅμιλον ‘throng’ as its object. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἳ δ’ ἄρα τοῦ μάλα μὲν κλύον ἠδὲ πίθοντο·
sentences.l: So he spoke, and they then readily heard him and obeyed.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and they listened to him readily and obeyed.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφαθ’ ‘so he spoke’ closes the speech, and οἳ δ’ ἄρα turns to the army, ‘and they then’. τοῦ ‘him’ is the genitive that goes with κλύον ‘heard (him)’, an unaugmented aorist; μάλα is ‘readily’, and πίθοντο the aorist of πείθομαι ‘obey’. The line is used elsewhere in the poem.

sentences.t:
οἳ μὲν ἄρ’ ἀμφ’ Αἴαντα καὶ Ἰδομενῆα ἄνακτα
Τεῦκρον Μηριόνην τε Μέγην τ’ ἀτάλαντον Ἄρηϊ
ὑσμίνην ἤρτυνον ἀριστῆας καλέσαντες
Ἕκτορι καὶ Τρώεσσιν ἐναντίον·
sentences.l:
These, then, around Ajax and Idomeneus, the lord,
Teucer, Meriones, and Meges, the equal of Ares,
set the battle in order, having called the best men
against Hector and the Trojans;
sentences.i: These men, around Ajax and lord Idomeneus, Teucer, Meriones, and Meges, the equal of Ares, set the battle in order, having called the best men to face Hector and the Trojans;
sentences.n: οἳ μὲν ἄρ’ ‘these, then’ are the Achaeans who obeyed, and the unit says what the leaders did. ἀμφί with the accusative puts the action ‘around’ the five named heroes: Ajax, lord Idomeneus, Teucer, Meriones and Meges. ἀτάλαντον Ἄρηϊ ‘the equal of Ares’ is the epithet of Meges. ὑσμίνην ἤρτυνον is ‘set the battle in order’, the imperfect of ἀρτύνω; ἀριστῆας καλέσαντες is ‘having called the best men’; and ἐναντίον ‘against’ takes the datives Ἕκτορι … Τρώεσσιν.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὀπίσσω
ἣ πληθὺς ἐπὶ νῆας Ἀχαιῶν ἀπονέοντο.
sentences.l:
but behind,
the multitude to the ships of the Achaeans went back.
sentences.i: while behind them the mass of the army went back to the ships of the Achaeans.
sentences.n: αὐτάρ ‘but’ turns from the leaders to the crowd, and ὀπίσσω is ‘behind’. ἣ is the article ‘the’. πληθύς is a singular collective noun, but ἀπονέοντο (imperfect of ἀπονέομαι ‘go back’) is plural, because the sense is the many men of the crowd. It is the verb already used in line 295.

sentences.t:
Τρῶες δὲ προὔτυψαν ἀολλέες, ἦρχε δ’ ἄρ’ Ἕκτωρ
μακρὰ βιβάς·
sentences.l:
And the Trojans pressed forward in a close mass, and led, then, Hector,
striding with long strides;
sentences.i: And the Trojans pressed forward in a close mass, with Hector leading them, striding with long strides;
sentences.n: Τρῶες δέ turns to the other side. προὔτυψαν (= προέτυψαν) is an aorist of προτύπτω ‘press forward’, and ἀολλέες ‘in a close mass’ is the word for ranks packed together. ἦρχε δ’ ἄρ’ Ἕκτωρ is ‘and Hector led’. μακρὰ βιβάς is the present participle of βίβημι ‘stride’ with the neuter plural as an adverb, ‘with long strides’.

sentences.t:
πρόσθεν δὲ κί’ αὐτοῦ Φοῖβος Ἀπόλλων
εἱμένος ὤμοιιν νεφέλην, ἔχε δ’ αἰγίδα θοῦριν
δεινὴν ἀμφιδάσειαν ἀριπρεπέ’, ἣν ἄρα χαλκεὺς
Ἥφαιστος Διὶ δῶκε φορήμεναι ἐς φόβον ἀνδρῶν·
sentences.l:
and before him went Phoebus Apollo,
clothed on his two shoulders in cloud, and held the aegis, impetuous,
dread, shaggy-all-round, outstanding, which then the smith
Hephaestus to Zeus gave to bear, for the flight of men;
sentences.i: and before him went Phoebus Apollo, wrapped in cloud about the shoulders, and he held the impetuous aegis, dread, shaggy all round, outstanding, which Hephaestus the smith gave to Zeus to carry, to put men to flight;
sentences.n: The god walks ahead of Hector: πρόσθεν … αὐτοῦ ‘before him’, and κί’ is κίε, the unaugmented imperfect of κίω ‘go’. εἱμένος is the perfect participle of ἕννυμι ‘clothe’, with νεφέλην ‘cloud’ as what he is wearing and ὤμοιιν (dual) ‘on his two shoulders’. αἰγίδα is the aegis, the emblem of Zeus that frightens men; θοῦριν ‘impetuous’, δεινήν ‘dread’, ἀμφιδάσειαν ‘shaggy all round’ (a rare word, from δασύς ‘shaggy’, perhaps for the tassels) and ἀριπρεπέ’ ‘outstanding’ all agree with it. δῶκε … φορήμεναι ‘gave to carry’ has the epic infinitive in -ήμεναι, and ἐς φόβον ἀνδρῶν is ‘for the flight of men’: φόβος in battle is the running that fear drives.

sentences.t: τὴν ἄρ’ ὅ γ’ ἐν χείρεσσιν ἔχων ἡγήσατο λαῶν.
sentences.l: this then he, in his hands holding, led the people.
sentences.i: Holding it in his hands, he led the people.
sentences.n: τήν ‘this’ picks up αἰγίδα and stands first for emphasis. ὅ γ’ is ‘he’, and it is Apollo, not Hector, who holds the aegis. ἔχων ‘holding’ goes with ἡγήσατο ‘led’, the aorist of ἡγέομαι, which takes the genitive λαῶν: ‘led the people’.

sentences.t:
Ἀργεῖοι δ’ ὑπέμειναν ἀολλέες, ὦρτο δ’ ἀϋτὴ
ὀξεῖ’ ἀμφοτέρωθεν, ἀπὸ νευρῆφι δ’ ὀϊστοὶ
θρῷσκον·
sentences.i: The Argives stood firm in a close mass, and a shrill battle-cry arose from both sides, and the arrows leapt from the bowstrings;
sentences.n: Ἀργεῖοι δ’ begins the Achaean side. ὑπέμειναν is the aorist of ὑπομένω ‘stand firm, hold one’s ground’, with no object. ὦρτο is the aorist middle of ὄρνυμι, ‘arose’; ἀϋτή is the ‘battle-cry’, ὀξεῖ’ (= ὀξεῖα) ‘shrill’, and ἀμφοτέρωθεν ‘from both sides’. In ἀπὸ νευρῆφι the ending -φι does the work of the genitive: ‘from the string’. θρῷσκον is the imperfect of θρῴσκω ‘leap’.

sentences.t:
πολλὰ δὲ δοῦρα θρασειάων ἀπὸ χειρῶν
ἄλλα μὲν ἐν χροῒ πήγνυτ’ ἀρηϊθόων αἰζηῶν,
πολλὰ δὲ καὶ μεσσηγὺ πάρος χρόα λευκὸν ἐπαυρεῖν
ἐν γαίῃ ἵσταντο λιλαιόμενα χροὸς ἆσαι.
sentences.l:
and many spears from bold hands
some in the flesh were fixed, of war-swift vigorous young men,
but many also midway, before the white flesh to touch,
in the earth stood, longing to glut themselves with flesh.
sentences.i: and many spears from bold hands, some of them stuck fast in the flesh of strong young men, swift in war, and many stood in the earth midway, before they could touch the white flesh, longing to glut themselves on it.
sentences.n: πολλὰ δὲ δοῦρα ‘and many spears’ is the subject of the whole sentence, and ἄλλα μέν … πολλὰ δέ splits it: some stuck in flesh, many fell short. θρασειάων … χειρῶν is the epic genitive plural ‘from bold hands’. πήγνυτ’ is the imperfect passive ‘were being fixed’, ἐν χροῒ ‘in the flesh’. ἀρηϊθόων αἰζηῶν ‘strong young men, swift in war’ is a formula whose first element is probably Ἄρης ‘war’. πάρος … ἐπαυρεῖν is ‘before they could touch’, with χρόα λευκόν ‘the white flesh’. λιλαιόμενα ‘longing’ takes the genitive χροός, and ἆσαι is the aorist infinitive ‘to glut’. The last two lines are used elsewhere of spears.

sentences.t:
ὄφρα μὲν αἰγίδα χερσὶν ἔχ’ ἀτρέμα Φοῖβος Ἀπόλλων,
τόφρα μάλ’ ἀμφοτέρων βέλε’ ἥπτετο, πῖπτε δὲ λαός.
sentences.l:
As long as in his hands held the aegis motionless Phoebus Apollo,
for that time the missiles of both sides took hold, and the people fell.
sentences.i: As long as Phoebus Apollo held the aegis motionless in his hands, for that time the missiles of both sides struck home, and the army fell.
sentences.n: ὄφρα μέν … τόφρα ‘as long as … for that time’ is a pair that measures one stretch of time. ἔχ’ is ἔχε ‘held’, the imperfect, and ἀτρέμα ‘motionless’ says that he did not shake the aegis. βέλε’ (= βέλεα) ‘missiles’ of ἀμφοτέρων ‘both sides’ is the subject of ἥπτετο, the middle of ἅπτω ‘take hold’: the volleys struck home. πῖπτε is the imperfect of πίπτω ‘fell’. The second line is used elsewhere in the poem.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ κατ’ ἐνῶπα ἰδὼν Δαναῶν ταχυπώλων
σεῖσ’, ἐπὶ δ’ αὐτὸς ἄϋσε μάλα μέγα, τοῖσι δὲ θυμὸν
ἐν στήθεσσιν ἔθελξε, λάθοντο δὲ θούριδος ἀλκῆς.
sentences.l:
But when, looking face to face at the swift-colted Danaans,
he shook it, and on them himself shouted very loudly, and their heart
in their breasts he enchanted, and they forgot impetuous might.
sentences.i: But when he looked the Danaans with their swift colts full in the face and shook it, and shouted at them very loudly himself, he enchanted the heart in their breasts, and they forgot their impetuous might.
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ἐπεί ‘but when’; the aegis is the object of σεῖσ’ (= σεῖσε, the unaugmented aorist of σείω ‘shook’) and is left unsaid. κατ’ ἐνῶπα ἰδών is ‘looking face to face’, and Δαναῶν ταχυπώλων ‘the swift-colted Danaans’ (the Danaans with swift colts) is the people he looks at. ἐπὶ … ἄϋσε is a split verb, ‘shouted at them’, and αὐτός ‘himself’ marks the god as the one who does it. θυμὸν ἐν στήθεσσιν ἔθελξε is ‘enchanted the heart in their breasts’ (θέλγω ‘enchant’, στήθεσσιν the epic dative plural). λάθοντο is the aorist of λανθάνομαι and takes the genitive θούριδος ἀλκῆς.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ὥς τ’ ἠὲ βοῶν ἀγέλην ἢ πῶϋ μέγ’ οἰῶν
θῆρε δύω κλονέωσι μελαίνης νυκτὸς ἀμολγῷ
ἐλθόντ’ ἐξαπίνης σημάντορος οὐ παρεόντος,
ὣς ἐφόβηθεν Ἀχαιοὶ ἀνάλκιδες·
sentences.l:
And they, as when a herd of cattle or a great flock of sheep
two wild beasts throw into confusion in the dead of black night,
having come suddenly, no order-giver being present,
so were put to flight the Achaeans, without might;
sentences.i: And as when two wild beasts come suddenly in the depths of black night and throw a herd of cattle or a great flock of sheep into confusion, with no herdsman there, so the Achaeans were put to flight, without might;
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ ὥς τ’ begins a simile that is finished only by ὣς ἐφόβηθεν ‘so were put to flight’ in line 326: the Achaeans are the herd or flock. κλονέωσι is the subjunctive of κλονέω ‘throw into confusion’, and θῆρε δύω ‘two wild beasts’ and ἐλθόντ’ are duals. In νυκτὸς ἀμολγῷ the meaning of ἀμολγός is not known (ancient guesses are ‘milking time’ and ‘darkness’), so ‘the depths of the night’ is a guess at the sense. σημάντορος οὐ παρεόντος is a genitive absolute, ‘with no order-giver present’, here the herdsman. ἐφόβηθεν is the passive aorist (= ἐφοβήθησαν), and ἀνάλκιδες is ‘without might’.

sentences.t:
ἐν γὰρ Ἀπόλλων
ἧκε φόβον, Τρωσὶν δὲ καὶ Ἕκτορι κῦδος ὄπαζεν.
sentences.l:
for into them Apollo
sent flight, and to the Trojans and to Hector glory he was granting.
sentences.i: for Apollo sent flight among them, and granted glory to the Trojans and to Hector.
sentences.n: ἐν γὰρ … ἧκε ‘for … sent in’: the preposition ἐν is split from the aorist ἧκε of ἵημι and means ‘into them’. φόβον is ‘flight’: in battle the running that fear drives, not the feeling itself (that is φύζα, ‘panic’, in line 366). Τρωσὶν … Ἕκτορι are datives, and ὄπαζεν is the imperfect of ὀπάζω ‘make follow, grant’, so ‘was granting’ glory (κῦδος) to the Trojans and to Hector.

sentences.t: ἔνθα δ’ ἀνὴρ ἕλεν ἄνδρα κεδασθείσης ὑσμίνης.
sentences.l: Then a man took a man, the battle having been scattered.
sentences.i: Then, with the battle scattered, a man killed a man.
sentences.n: ἔνθα is ‘then’. ἕλεν is the unaugmented aorist of αἱρέω, literally ‘took’ and in battle ‘killed’; ἀνὴρ … ἄνδρα sets the two men side by side, one man killing one. κεδασθείσης ὑσμίνης ‘the battle having been scattered’ is a genitive absolute: the line has broken up into single fights, and the next lines list the dead.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτωρ μὲν Στιχίον τε καὶ Ἀρκεσίλαον ἔπεφνε,
τὸν μὲν Βοιωτῶν ἡγήτορα χαλκοχιτώνων,
τὸν δὲ Μενεσθῆος μεγαθύμου πιστὸν ἑταῖρον·
sentences.i: Hector killed Stichius and Arcesilaus, the one a leader of the bronze-shirted Boeotians, the other a trusty companion of great-hearted Menestheus;
sentences.n: Ἕκτωρ μέν begins a list of the dead; Aeneas’s kills follow in line 332 with δέ. Στιχίον and Ἀρκεσίλαον are the two accusatives, objects of ἔπεφνε ‘killed’. τὸν μέν … τὸν δέ are ‘the one … the other’, and they take the two names in reverse order: Arcesilaus is a Boeotian leader (he is in the Catalogue, 2.495), and Stichius is Menestheus’s comrade. χαλκοχιτώνων ‘bronze-shirted’ and μεγαθύμου ‘great-hearted’ are stock epithets, and πιστὸν ἑταῖρον is ‘trusty companion’.

sentences.t: Αἰνείας δὲ Μέδοντα καὶ Ἴασον ἐξενάριξεν.
sentences.l: and Aeneas Medon and Iasus despoiled.
sentences.i: and Aeneas killed Medon and Iasus and stripped them of their armour.
sentences.n: Αἰνείας is the nominative ‘Aeneas’, and Μέδοντα and Ἴασον are the accusatives of Medon and Iasus; the next lines say who they were. ἐξενάριξεν is the aorist of ἐξεναρίζω, ‘kill and strip’, from ἔναρα ‘spoils stripped from the slain’.

sentences.t:
ἤτοι ὃ μὲν νόθος υἱὸς Ὀϊλῆος θείοιο
ἔσκε Μέδων Αἴαντος ἀδελφεός·
sentences.l:
Now he, for his part, bastard son of divine Oileus,
was Medon, brother of Ajax;
sentences.i: Medon, for his part, was an illegitimate son of divine Oileus, and a brother of Ajax;
sentences.n: ἤτοι ὃ μὲν is ‘now he, for his part’: ἤτοι is printed as one word, and ὅ is the pronoun ‘he’. This begins a short life of Medon. νόθος ‘illegitimate’ means born outside marriage, and Ὀϊλῆος is the epic genitive of Oileus. ἔσκε is the iterative imperfect of εἰμί, here a plain ‘was’. Αἴαντος is the lesser Ajax, Oileus’s son, so Medon is his half-brother by another mother.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἔναιεν
ἐν Φυλάκῃ γαίης ἄπο πατρίδος ἄνδρα κατακτὰς
γνωτὸν μητρυιῆς Ἐριώπιδος, ἣν ἔχ’ Ὀϊλεύς·
sentences.i: but he lived in Phylace, away from his fatherland, after killing a man, a kinsman of his stepmother Eriopis, whom Oileus had as his wife;
sentences.n: αὐτάρ ‘but’ turns to Medon’s exile. ἔναιεν is the imperfect of ναίω ‘dwell’, and Φυλάκῃ is Phylace, a town. γαίης ἄπο πατρίδος has the preposition after its noun: ‘away from his native land’. κατακτάς is the short aorist participle of κατακτείνω ‘kill’, and γνωτόν ‘kinsman’ stands beside ἄνδρα for the man he killed. μητρυιῆς is ‘stepmother’, Ἐριώπιδος her name, and ἔχ’ is ἔχε, ‘had’ (as his wife).

sentences.t:
Ἴασος αὖτ’ ἀρχὸς μὲν Ἀθηναίων ἐτέτυκτο,
υἱὸς δὲ Σφήλοιο καλέσκετο Βουκολίδαο.
sentences.l:
Iasus, in turn, a commander of the Athenians was,
and a son of Sphelus, Bucolus’ son, he was called.
sentences.i: Iasus, for his part, was a commander of the Athenians, and was called the son of Sphelus, son of Bucolus.
sentences.n: Ἴασος αὖτ’ is ‘Iasus, in turn’, and ἀρχὸς μέν … υἱὸς δέ sets his office against his parentage. ἀρχός ‘commander’ takes the genitive Ἀθηναίων. ἐτέτυκτο is the pluperfect passive of τεύχω, ‘had been made’, which in use comes to mean ‘was’. καλέσκετο is the imperfect passive of καλέω in the -σκ- form, which marks repetition; the English keeps only ‘was called’. Σφήλοιο is the genitive of Sphelus, and Βουκολίδαο the epic patronymic ‘son of Bucolus’ agreeing with it.

sentences.t:
Μηκιστῆ δ’ ἕλε Πουλυδάμας, Ἐχίον δὲ Πολίτης
πρώτῃ ἐν ὑσμίνῃ, Κλονίον δ’ ἕλε δῖος Ἀγήνωρ.
sentences.l:
Mecisteus Polydamas took, and Echius Polites
in the foremost battle, and Clonius took heavenly Agenor.
sentences.i: Polydamas killed Mecisteus, and Polites Echius, in the front line of battle, and heavenly Agenor killed Clonius.
sentences.n: Μηκιστῆ is the accusative of Μηκιστεύς, ‘Mecisteus’, and Πουλυδάμας is the subject of ἕλε ‘took’, ‘killed’. Πολίτης has no verb of its own: ἕλε is understood, and Ἐχίον is the accusative of Echius. πρώτῃ ἐν ὑσμίνῃ ‘in the foremost battle’ is the front line. Κλονίον δ’ ἕλε δῖος Ἀγήνωρ repeats the pattern, with the stock epithet δῖος ‘heavenly’.

sentences.t:
Δηΐοχον δὲ Πάρις βάλε νείατον ὦμον ὄπισθε
φεύγοντ’ ἐν προμάχοισι, διὰ πρὸ δὲ χαλκὸν ἔλασσεν.
sentences.l:
And Deiochus Paris struck, the lowest part of the shoulder, from behind,
as he fled among the front-fighters, and right through drove the bronze.
sentences.i: And Paris struck Deiochus in the lowest part of the shoulder from behind as he fled among the foremost fighters, and drove the bronze right through.
sentences.n: Δηΐοχον is the accusative of Deiochus, Πάρις the subject, and βάλε ‘struck’ the aorist of βάλλω. νείατον ὦμον: νείατος is ‘lowest’, and the accusative names the part struck, ‘in the lowest part of the shoulder’. ὄπισθε is ‘from behind’, and φεύγοντ’ the participle ‘as he fled’. ἐν προμάχοισι is ‘among the front-fighters’. διὰ πρὸ … ἔλασσεν is a split verb, ‘drove right through’, the aorist of ἐλαύνω, and χαλκόν ‘the bronze’ is the weapon’s point.

sentences.t:
ὄφρ’ οἳ τοὺς ἐνάριζον ἀπ’ ἔντεα, τόφρα δ’ Ἀχαιοὶ
τάφρῳ καὶ σκολόπεσσιν ἐνιπλήξαντες ὀρυκτῇ
ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα φέβοντο, δύοντο δὲ τεῖχος ἀνάγκῃ.
sentences.l:
While they were despoiling those men of their gear, meanwhile the Achaeans,
into ditch and stakes having dashed, the dug one,
this way and that fled, and went into the wall by necessity.
sentences.i: While they were stripping the dead of their gear, the Achaeans meanwhile dashed into the dug ditch and the stakes, fled this way and that, and went into the wall of necessity.
sentences.n: ὄφρ’ … τόφρα ‘while … meanwhile’ pairs two scenes: the Trojans strip the dead, the Achaeans run. οἳ ‘they’ are the Trojans and τούς ‘those’ the fallen. ἐνάριζον is the imperfect of ἐναρίζω, with ἀπ’ (= ἀπό) split from it, ‘stripped off’, and ἔντεα ‘gear’ is what they take. ἐνιπλήξαντες is the aorist participle of ἐνιπλήσσω ‘dash into’, with the datives τάφρῳ … ὀρυκτῇ ‘the dug ditch’ and σκολόπεσσιν ‘stakes’. δύοντο … τεῖχος is ‘went into the wall’, and ἀνάγκῃ ‘by necessity’.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτωρ δὲ Τρώεσσιν ἐκέκλετο μακρὸν ἀΰσας
νηυσὶν ἐπισσεύεσθαι, ἐᾶν δ’ ἔναρα βροτόεντα·
sentences.l:
And Hector to the Trojans called out, shouting loudly,
to rush upon the ships, and to leave the bloody spoils;
sentences.i: And Hector gave orders to the Trojans, shouting loudly, to rush upon the ships and to leave the bloody spoils alone;
sentences.n: Ἕκτωρ δὲ … ἐκέκλετο ‘and Hector called out, gave orders’ is a line the poet uses for other speakers too. The orders are reported in indirect speech, with the infinitives ἐπισσεύεσθαι ‘to rush upon’ (νηυσίν ‘the ships’, dative) and ἐᾶν ‘to leave’. ἔναρα βροτόεντα ‘bloody spoils’ means the armour taken from the dead. Hector’s own words begin in the next unit.

sentences.t:
ὃν δ’ ἂν ἐγὼν ἀπάνευθε νεῶν ἑτέρωθι νοήσω,
αὐτοῦ οἱ θάνατον μητίσομαι,
sentences.l:
“And whomever I shall perceive apart from the ships, elsewhere,
right there for him I will devise death,
sentences.i: “And whomever I see apart from the ships, off elsewhere, right there I will devise death for him,
sentences.n: ὃν δ’ ἂν … νοήσω is ‘and whomever I shall perceive’, with ἄν and the aorist subjunctive for a general case. ἀπάνευθε νεῶν ἑτέρωθι is ‘apart from the ships, elsewhere’. αὐτοῦ ‘on the spot’, οἱ is the dative ‘for him’, and θάνατον μητίσομαι is ‘I will devise death’, from μητίομαι (related to μῆτις ‘cunning’).

sentences.t:
οὐδέ νυ τόν γε
γνωτοί τε γνωταί τε πυρὸς λελάχωσι θανόντα,
ἀλλὰ κύνες ἐρύουσι πρὸ ἄστεος ἡμετέροιο.
sentences.l:
nor him at all, at least,
kinsmen and kinswomen will give a share of fire, when dead,
but dogs will drag him before our city.”
sentences.i: and his kinsmen and kinswomen will not give him, dead, his share of fire; no, dogs will drag him before our city.”
sentences.n: οὐδέ νυ τόν γε is ‘and not him, at all’: τόν is the object, and θανόντα ‘dead’ agrees with it. λελάχωσι is the reduplicated aorist subjunctive of λαγχάνω, which in this phrase means ‘give a share’; the share of fire is the funeral pyre. γνωτοί … γνωταί are ‘kinsmen and kinswomen’ (γνωτός ‘kinsman’ and its feminine plural). κύνες ‘dogs’ is the subject of ἐρύουσι ‘they drag’, a present with the force of a future, and πρὸ ἄστεος ἡμετέροιο is ‘before our city’. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς εἰπὼν μάστιγι κατωμαδὸν ἤλασεν ἵππους
κεκλόμενος Τρώεσσι κατὰ στίχας·
sentences.l:
So having spoken, with the whip from the shoulder he drove the horses,
calling on the Trojans along the ranks;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and drove his horses on with the whip, laid on from the shoulder, calling to the Trojans along the ranks;
sentences.n: ὣς εἰπών ‘so having spoken’ ends Hector’s speech. μάστιγι is the dative ‘with the whip’, and κατωμαδόν is a rare adverb, ‘from the shoulder’, the arm swung with its whole weight. ἤλασεν ‘drove’ is the aorist of ἐλαύνω, with ἵππους ‘horses’ as its object. κεκλόμενος ‘calling on’ takes the dative Τρώεσσι, and κατὰ στίχας is ‘along the ranks’.

sentences.t:
οἳ δὲ σὺν αὐτῷ
πάντες ὁμοκλήσαντες ἔχον ἐρυσάρματας ἵππους
ἠχῇ θεσπεσίῃ·
sentences.i: and all those with him shouted and drove on their chariot-drawing horses with a wondrous din;
sentences.n: οἳ δέ ‘and they’ are the Trojans, σὺν αὐτῷ ‘with him’. ὁμοκλήσαντες is the aorist participle of ὁμοκλάω ‘shout at’, used here with no object. ἔχον ‘held, kept on’ is the imperfect of ἔχω. ἐρυσάρματας ‘chariot-drawing’ (from ἐρύω ‘draw’ and ἅρμα ‘chariot’) agrees with ἵππους, and ἠχῇ θεσπεσίῃ is ‘with a wondrous din’.

sentences.t:
προπάροιθε δὲ Φοῖβος Ἀπόλλων
ῥεῖ’ ὄχθας καπέτοιο βαθείης ποσσὶν ἐρείπων
ἐς μέσσον κατέβαλλε,
sentences.l:
and in front Phoebus Apollo,
easily the banks of the deep ditch with his feet bringing down,
threw them into the middle,
sentences.i: and in front of them Phoebus Apollo easily brought down the banks of the deep ditch with his feet and threw them into the middle,
sentences.n: Apollo now does his work on the ditch. προπάροιθε is ‘in front’, and ῥεῖ’ is ῥεῖα ‘easily’. ὄχθας καπέτοιο βαθείης is ‘the banks of the deep ditch’, ποσσὶν the epic dative plural ‘with his feet’. ἐρείπων is the participle of ἐρείπω, which usually means ‘crash down’ and here has an object. κατέβαλλε is the imperfect of καταβάλλω ‘throw down’, and ἐς μέσσον ‘into the middle’ means into the ditch itself.

sentences.t:
γεφύρωσεν δὲ κέλευθον
μακρὴν ἠδ’ εὐρεῖαν, ὅσον τ’ ἐπὶ δουρὸς ἐρωὴ
γίγνεται, ὁππότ’ ἀνὴρ σθένεος πειρώμενος ᾗσι.
sentences.l:
and bridged a way
long and wide, as great as the rush of a spear
is, when a man trying his strength throws it.
sentences.i: and bridged a way, long and wide, as far as the rush of a spear goes when a man throws it, testing his strength.
sentences.n: γεφύρωσεν is the aorist of γεφυρόω ‘bridge’, from γέφυρα ‘bridge’, and κέλευθον ‘way’ with μακρὴν ἠδ’ εὐρεῖαν ‘long and wide’ is the causeway the filled ditch makes. ὅσον τ’ ἐπὶ … ἐρωή is ‘as far as the rush … goes’: ἐρωή is the rush or carry of a thrown spear, with δουρός in the genitive. ὁππότ’ ἀνὴρ … ᾗσι is ‘whenever a man throws’, ᾗσι being the aorist subjunctive of ἵημι, and σθένεος πειρώμενος ‘testing his strength’ takes the genitive.

sentences.t:
τῇ ῥ’ οἵ γε προχέοντο φαλαγγηδόν, πρὸ δ’ Ἀπόλλων
αἰγίδ’ ἔχων ἐρίτιμον·
sentences.l:
There they poured forth in phalanx-fashion, and before them Apollo
holding the much-honoured aegis;
sentences.i: That way they poured forward in a phalanx, and in front of them Apollo, holding the much honoured aegis;
sentences.n: τῇ is ‘that way’, ῥ’ is ἄρα, and οἵ γε ‘they’ are the Trojans. προχέοντο is the imperfect passive of προχέω ‘pour forth’, and φαλαγγηδόν ‘in a phalanx’ is an adverb in -δόν. πρὸ δ’ Ἀπόλλων has no verb, ‘and in front, Apollo’, and ἔχων … αἰγίδ’ ἐρίτιμον ‘holding the much honoured aegis’ goes with it.

sentences.t:
ἔρειπε δὲ τεῖχος Ἀχαιῶν
ῥεῖα μάλ’, ὡς ὅτε τις ψάμαθον πάϊς ἄγχι θαλάσσης,
ὅς τ’ ἐπεὶ οὖν ποιήσῃ ἀθύρματα νηπιέῃσιν
ἂψ αὖτις συνέχευε ποσὶν καὶ χερσὶν ἀθύρων.
sentences.l:
and he was bringing down the wall of the Achaeans
very easily, as when some child sand near the sea,
who, when he has made playthings in his childishness,
again, back once more, jumbles together with feet and hands, playing.
sentences.i: and he brought down the wall of the Achaeans very easily, as a child does with sand beside the sea: once he has made his playthings in his childish way, he tumbles them back into a jumble again with his feet and hands, in play.
sentences.n: ἔρειπε ‘was bringing down’ is the imperfect of ἐρείπω, the verb of line 356, and τεῖχος Ἀχαιῶν ‘the wall of the Achaeans’ is its object. ῥεῖα μάλ’ is ‘very easily’. The simile ὡς ὅτε τις … πάϊς ‘as when some child’ is loose in its grammar: ψάμαθον ‘sand’ has no verb of its own, and the sense is that the child plays with it. ποιήσῃ is the aorist subjunctive in a general clause, ‘when he has made’, ἀθύρματα ‘playthings’ (from ἀθύρω ‘play’) and νηπιέῃσιν ‘in his childishness’. συνέχευε is the aorist of συγχέω, used for what always happens, ‘he jumbles together’, and ἀθύρων ‘playing’ is its participle.

sentences.t:
ὥς ῥα σὺ ἤϊε Φοῖβε πολὺν κάματον καὶ ὀϊζὺν
σύγχεας Ἀργείων, αὐτοῖσι δὲ φύζαν ἐνῶρσας.
sentences.l:
So then you, Ēïe Phoebus, much toil and distress
of the Argives confounded, and in them themselves panic you roused.
sentences.i: So, Phoebus, you undid the great toil and distress of the Argives, and stirred up panic in the men themselves.
sentences.n: The poet speaks to Apollo directly: ὥς ῥα σὺ … Φοῖβε ‘so then you, Phoebus’. ἤϊε is a vocative epithet of Apollo whose meaning is not known, so it is left untranslated in the literal line and dropped from the free English. κάματον ‘toil’ and ὀϊζύν ‘distress’ are probably what the Argives had spent on the wall. σύγχεας is the unaugmented aorist of συγχέω ‘jumble together, confound’, the verb of the child in the line before. αὐτοῖσι ‘in them themselves’ is set against the toil, φύζαν is ‘panic’, and ἐνῶρσας the aorist of ἐνόρνυμι ‘stir up in’.

sentences.t:
ὣς οἳ μὲν παρὰ νηυσὶν ἐρητύοντο μένοντες,
ἀλλήλοισί τε κεκλόμενοι καὶ πᾶσι θεοῖσι
χεῖρας ἀνίσχοντες μεγάλ’ εὐχετόωντο ἕκαστος·
sentences.i: So these held where they were beside the ships, standing fast, calling on one another and on all the gods, and each man lifted up his hands and prayed loudly;
sentences.n: ὣς οἳ μὲν ‘so these’ turns to the Achaeans by the ships. ἐρητύοντο is the imperfect passive of ἐρητύω ‘hold back’, and μένοντες ‘remaining’ goes with it: they were held, and stayed where they were. κεκλόμενοι ‘calling on’ takes both ἀλλήλοισι ‘one another’ and θεοῖσι ‘gods’. ἀνίσχοντες is ‘lifting up’, and εὐχετόωντο the imperfect of εὐχετάομαι ‘pray’ with the epic ending -όωντο; μεγάλ’ is the neuter plural as an adverb, ‘loudly’. Lines 368 and 369 are used elsewhere in the poem.

sentences.t:
Νέστωρ αὖτε μάλιστα Γερήνιος οὖρος Ἀχαιῶν
εὔχετο χεῖρ’ ὀρέγων εἰς οὐρανὸν ἀστερόεντα·
sentences.l:
And Nestor, in turn, most of all, the Gerenian, warden of the Achaeans,
prayed, stretching out his hands to the starry sky:
sentences.i: And Nestor, the Gerenian, warden of the Achaeans, prayed most of all, stretching out his hands to the starry sky:
sentences.n: Νέστωρ αὖτε is ‘Nestor, in turn’, and μάλιστα ‘most of all’ goes with the praying. Γερήνιος is his stock epithet, of uncertain meaning, and οὖρος is ‘warden, guardian’ (not the other οὖρος ‘fair wind’). εὔχετο is the imperfect of εὔχομαι ‘pray’, and ὀρέγων ‘stretching out’ takes χεῖρ’ ‘hands’; οὐρανὸν ἀστερόεντα is ‘the starry sky’. Line 371 is also used in the Odyssey. Nestor’s prayer follows.

sentences.t:
Ζεῦ πάτερ εἴ ποτέ τίς τοι ἐν Ἄργεΐ περ πολυπύρῳ
ἢ βοὸς ἢ οἰὸς κατὰ πίονα μηρία καίων
εὔχετο νοστῆσαι, σὺ δ’ ὑπέσχεο καὶ κατένευσας,
sentences.l:
“Father Zeus, if ever any man for you in Argos, rich in wheat,
either of ox or of sheep, the fat thigh-pieces burning,
prayed to return home, and you promised and nodded assent,
sentences.i: “Father Zeus, if ever any man in Argos, rich in wheat, burned for you the fat thigh-pieces of an ox or a sheep and prayed to return home, and you gave your promise and nodded your assent,
sentences.n: Ζεῦ πάτερ is ‘Father Zeus’. The prayer rests on a condition: εἴ ποτέ τίς τοι … εὔχετο is ‘if ever anyone … prayed to you’, with τοι = σοι. πολυπύρῳ ‘rich in wheat’ describes Ἄργεϊ (in Argos), with περ giving the place stress. ἢ βοὸς ἢ οἰὸς is ‘either of ox or of sheep’, the genitive of the animal whose thigh-pieces (μηρία) are burned, and κατὰ … καίων is a split verb, ‘burning’. νοστῆσαι is the aorist infinitive ‘to return home’ after εὔχετο. ὑπέσχεο ‘you promised’ and κατένευσας ‘you nodded assent’ are aorists addressed to Zeus.

sentences.t:
τῶν μνῆσαι καὶ ἄμυνον Ὀλύμπιε νηλεὲς ἦμαρ,
μηδ’ οὕτω Τρώεσσιν ἔα δάμνασθαι Ἀχαιούς.
sentences.l:
of those things remember, and ward off, Olympian, the pitiless day,
and not thus by the Trojans allow to be subdued the Achaeans.”
sentences.i: remember them, and ward off the pitiless day, Olympian, and do not let the Achaeans be subdued by the Trojans like this.”
sentences.n: τῶν μνῆσαι ‘remember those things’ is an imperative: μνῆσαι is the aorist middle of μιμνῄσκομαι, which takes the genitive τῶν, the promises just named. ἄμυνον ‘ward off’ is the aorist imperative of ἀμύνω, with νηλεὲς ἦμαρ ‘the pitiless day’ as its object, and Ὀλύμπιε ‘Olympian’ is the vocative. μηδ’ οὕτω … ἔα is ‘and do not thus allow’: ἔα is the imperative of ἐάω, and Ἀχαιούς with the infinitive δάμνασθαι ‘to be subdued’ is its object, the Trojans (Τρώεσσιν) the agent. The line is used elsewhere in the poem. The prayer ends here.
